justification_text:
At the time of this forecast, the point estimates across all three horizons were clustered tightly around 29.2 to 29.5, suggesting I was modeling a relatively stable underlying variable with modest drift. The 1-day estimate of 29.2 was anchored primarily to the most recent observed value, with very little expected movement over such a short window. The slight upward drift to 29.3 at one week and 29.5 at one month likely reflected a mild positive trend in the underlying data — perhaps a slow-moving mean reversion, a gradual price appreciation, or a slowly rising indicator — rather than any sharp directional signal. The point estimates essentially assumed that whatever process was generating the data would continue along its recent trajectory without a major regime shift.

The confidence interval widths grew predictably with the time horizon, which is standard for most forecasting frameworks. At one day, the 90% CI of 28.5 to 29.9 is quite tight, spanning only 1.4 units, reflecting the high short-run autocorrelation typical of most financial or economic time series. By one month, the interval widens to 26.5 to 32.5 — a spread of 6 units — capturing the compounding uncertainty that accumulates as the forecast horizon extends. The width choices were likely informed by historical volatility or variance in the series, scaled appropriately by the square root of time or a similar heuristic. This implies an annualized volatility that was moderate but not negligible.

Several sources of uncertainty could push realized outcomes outside these stated intervals. At the 1-day horizon, a surprise announcement, data release, or liquidity shock could easily breach the narrow CI. At the 1-week and 1-month horizons, the risks broaden considerably — macroeconomic shifts, policy changes, geopolitical events, or structural breaks in the underlying series could all generate moves well outside the stated bounds. The 90% CI by construction admits a 10% chance of being violated, and in practice, tail events tend to cluster in time, meaning a single adverse week could invalidate both the 1-week and 1-month intervals simultaneously.

It is also worth acknowledging that these estimates carry model uncertainty on top of the stated statistical uncertainty. If the underlying series experienced a regime change — say, a transition from low to high volatility — then the historical variance used to calibrate interval widths would be too narrow, making the stated CIs overconfident. Similarly, if there were latent seasonal patterns or calendar effects not accounted for, the point estimates themselves could be systematically biased. Users of this forecast should treat the intervals as a useful guide to the central tendency of risk, not as hard probabilistic guarantees.
